title: Is Michael Corleone a hero or a villain by the end of the series?

commenti.body:
Villain. He looses his way. He starts off with a strong moral compass; he’s a war hero, he went to an Ivy League college and he wants nothing to do with the family business. He tries to take things in a legitimate direction but doesn’t. With all his wealth and power you’d think that would be a somewhat easy task but isn’t. His relationship with Kay starts off kind and loving but devolves into being distant and cruel. She recognizes it and leaves him. 

Fredo is a weak guy, he was clearly manipulated by Johnny Ola and Roth. Everyone begs Michael to forgive him but he doesn’t. 

Michael is a sympathetic bad guy but he’s a bad guy.

>On one hand, Michael can be seen as a hero due to his initial intention to protect his family and lead them to legitimate business, showcasing loyalty and a desire to honor his father's legacy. 

His father's legacy is one of bloodshed and corruption. Definitely a villian from about the last hour of *The Godfather* going forward.
Look what they did to my boy.

Worse than either: he’s a loser.

He wins the battle and loses the war. The line in the sand is in the conversation with his mother 

“Oh Michael you can never lose your family”

“Tempi cambiano”

He got the “family” bigger than US steel. In the interim: his dad died, his mom died, his brother died, he kills his other brother for betrayal, his sisters an embarrassment, his wife leaves him, his wife has an abortion (which was the ultimate power grab by Kaye and the punishment Michael deserved), he loses the love of his children.

It didn’t matter what he was. He was nothing anymore. That’s where the

You're not using the right frame. There are no heroes or villains. 

It's a Tragedy Play, basically, and Michael is the main character. You watch the Godfather to see that Michael's rise of power, prominence, and social esteem is paralleled by his moral decay, his choices to (literally) destroy his family, and his introversion of all knowledge, discussion, and decision-making.

I appreciate the commentary but in a way its like asking if Macbeth is a hero or a villain. 

The Godfather is like a Greek or Shakespearian tragedy where you follow a compelling protagonist with sparks of greatness but who eventually destroy everything and everyone around them. 

The irony is that so many people seemingly idolize and romanticize mobsters and the mafia when movies like the Godfather are meant to show the utter absurdity and destructiveness of that life. 

The glamor, the power, the excitement of seeing Michael triumph over his enemies is the seductive hook to get the audience to see what makes that life so compelling to the criminals who engage in it. 

However, I believe we are ultimately expected to see it for what it is, a farce of honor covering up violence, moral decay, and human misery. 

I suppose the fact that some people see Michael and others in the genre as heroes shows why such people still exist in this world.

He's a villain, pretty much from the moment he shoots McCluskey, but the theme in the movie is not heroes and villains, it's winners and losers, and the main point of the movie is that by the end, he has won everything (money, power) and at the same time he's lost everything that matters (love, trust, self respect)

>father's legacy.

Vito Corleone was a criminal. 

> His strategic mind and leadership skills enable him to navigate and control a world rife with danger and corruption, ostensibly for the sake of those he loves.

I don't think Michael makes any choices based on other people's needs. 

I was originally going to say that Michael's decision to kill McCluskey (sp?) is the only time he puts his family's needs over his own but after typing it out I think he killed McCluskey because McCluskey broke his jaw and called him a name. 


I think Michael is very good at justifying personal revenge and choices that advance his personal advantage by calling it "business." We watch him trade the health, safety, and freedom of other people - including his brothers - for those advantages. Outside the McCluskey hit, he never takes the fall. 

>interpreted as both heroic and villainous

The classical definition of a villain is a character "whose evil actions or motives are important to the plot." Michael fits that definition.

> he never lost his family in pursuit of an empire

I take your point but Vito did lose his family.

He lost Sonny and Fredo.

He lost his dream of legitimizing Michael.

He was long dead when Fredo died. When Vito passed he was at the compound surrounded by real and mob family. 

When Michael wins out, his home is empty. 

Idk about the dream of legitimizing Michael, I doubt he imagined he’d live long enough to see Michael become a senator but he was broken when Michael made the hit

> When Vito passed he was at the compound surrounded by real and mob family.

Who all died tragically because of his plans.
